reading: Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter will form a line in the sky before sunrise throughout November.
All four planets will be visible to the naked eye, so viewers will not need a telescope to see them.
Mercury will be the hardest of the four planets to spot.
It will look dim and remain near the horizon, the line where the sky appears to meet the ground.
Venus will appear above Mercury and to its right.
Venus, which reflects a high proportion of sunlight, is the brightest object in the night sky after the Moon.
On 15 and 16 November, Mars and Jupiter will appear very near each other in the sky.
According to astronomer Gideon Bendavid-Walker, the gap between them will be roughly the width of a finger held at arm’s length.
The pair will appear near the star Regulus, and the three objects may look like a group of three stars.
Viewers should choose a place away from light pollution, meaning artificial light that makes the night sky harder to see.
They should find an open view of the eastern horizon and allow around twenty minutes for their eyes to adjust to the dark.
The best viewing time is approximately 45 to 60 minutes before sunrise.
